blocks.prompt: Two Kinds of Balloons
blocks.text: A balloon is just a bag of stretchy rubber. When you blow into it, your breath pushes the rubber out. The rubber pulls back in. That is why a balloon feels tight in your hands. Look around at a party. Some balloons roll on the floor. Some balloons pull up at the end of a string. They are made of the same rubber. What is inside them is not the same. The floor balloons are full of your breath. The string balloons are full of a gas called helium. Helium is lighter than the air in the room, so the balloon goes up.

blocks.prompt: A Balloon Starts as Sap
blocks.text: A balloon begins its life as a drip. In a warm forest, a worker cuts a curved line into the bark of a rubber tree. A white liquid called latex slides down the cut and drops into a little cup. That sticky sap is the balloon before it is a balloon. At a factory, a machine dips a balloon shaped mold into a tank of latex, lifts it out, and dips it again, until a thin rubber skin has built up. The skin is peeled off, and there it is. Flat, floppy, and waiting for air. Now think about the two kinds of balloons at a party. The ones you blow up yourself sink to the floor. The ones on strings tug toward the ceiling. Same rubber, different gas. The floating ones are filled with helium, and helium is lighter than the air in the room. The heavier air crowds in underneath and shoves the balloon upward. Nothing is pulling that balloon up. The air is pushing it up from below.

a mold is dipped in latex over and over until a thin skin builds up
helium is lighter than air, so the heavier air pushes it up from below
(inference: your breath is heavier than helium, so the air cannot push it up)

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Michael Faraday made the first rubber balloon in 1824
It was lab equipment, not a toy
Rubber is made of long molecules called chains
Helium travels as a single atom, not a pair
That is why helium balloons sag first

blocks.prompt: Faraday's Bag of Hydrogen
blocks.text: Nobody set out to invent the party balloon. In 1824, a scientist named Michael Faraday was experimenting with hydrogen in a London laboratory and needed a container light enough to hold it. He cut two circles of rubber, pressed the rims together, and dusted flour on the inside so the sheets would not glue themselves shut. The balloon was a piece of lab equipment. Within a year someone was selling the idea as a toy, and it has stayed a toy ever since. The reason a balloon works at all is hidden inside the rubber. Rubber is built from molecules so long that scientists call them chains. When the balloon is limp, those chains lie tangled and coiled like noodles in a bowl. Blow into it and you drag the chains straight. Straight chains are unhappy chains. They pull to coil up again, and that pull is what presses back on your fingers and keeps the air squeezed tight. Let go of the neck and the chains snap home all at once, firing your breath out in a rude squeal. Here is something you may have noticed. A helium balloon is sagging by the next morning, while a balloon full of your own breath can stay round for a week. The rubber has not failed. A balloon skin is not solid the way a wall is solid, and it has gaps far too small to see. The gases in your breath travel as pairs of atoms locked together. Helium travels alone, one small atom at a time, and a lone helium atom can slip between the rubber chains and wander off into the room. The balloon is not leaking. It is being escaped from.

notes: Helium was found in the sun in 1868, before anyone found it on Earth
Named for Helios, the Greek sun
Earth's helium is made by radioactive rock, atom by atom
It is trapped underground with natural gas
Released helium leaves the planet for good
Liquid helium cools the magnets inside MRI scanners

blocks.prompt: The Gas We Found in the Sun
blocks.text: The gas inside a floating balloon has a stranger history than the balloon does. In 1868, astronomers pointed their instruments at an eclipse and split the sun's light into a band of colors. Sitting in that band was a bright yellow line that matched no element anyone had on a shelf. They had discovered something in the sun before finding a single atom of it on Earth, so they named it after Helios, the Greek word for the sun. Helium was a rumor from ninety three million miles away for another twenty seven years before a chemist finally coaxed it out of a rock in a London laboratory. That rock is the clue. Earth did not arrive with much helium, and what little it had drifted away long ago. The helium we use is manufactured underground, slowly, by radioactive elements like uranium and thorium as they break down inside the crust. Each decay spits out a particle that is, in effect, a single helium atom. Over hundreds of millions of years these atoms seep upward and collect in the same porous rock traps that hold natural gas, and that is where we drill for them. Helium is not grown, farmed, or manufactured in a factory. It is mined, and the supply took longer to make than mammals have existed. Now consider what happens when a balloon lets go. Helium is so light that once it is loose in the atmosphere, nothing holds it down. It rises past the weather, past the airplanes, and eventually the atoms at the very top of the atmosphere are moving fast enough to leave. They do not fall back. They are gone from the planet permanently. Almost every other resource we waste stays on Earth somewhere, buried or floating or piled up, waiting to be recovered by somebody smarter than us. Helium is the exception. Meanwhile, liquid helium is the coldest practical substance we have, and it is what keeps the magnets inside an MRI scanner cold enough to work. There is no substitute. So a balloon is a small, cheerful, faintly ridiculous thing: a party decoration inflated with a finite gas that took the crust of the Earth a hundred million years to brew, and that leaves the planet forever the moment a child lets go of the string.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Weather balloons launch worldwide at 00 and 12 UTC
Roughly 900 stations, twice every day
They carry a radiosonde: sensors plus a radio
They climb near 100,000 feet, into the stratosphere
The balloon swells from about 6 feet to over 20 feet across
Then it bursts, on purpose, every single time

blocks.prompt: The Balloon Whose Job Is to Burst
blocks.text: Twice a day, at the same two moments on the clock, roughly nine hundred people scattered across the planet walk outdoors and let go of a balloon. They do it at midnight and at noon Coordinated Universal Time, so that every launch happens together, from the Antarctic ice to the middle of the Pacific to a field behind a weather office in Nebraska. It is the largest coordinated act of measurement humans perform, and it runs on a bag of latex. The balloon leaves the ground about six feet across, filled with helium or hydrogen, trailing a string with a small white box on the end. That box is a radiosonde, and it is the entire point. Inside are a thermometer, a humidity sensor, a pressure sensor, a GPS receiver, a battery, and a radio. As the balloon climbs at around a thousand feet a minute, the sonde reads the atmosphere continuously and radios its numbers back down. The wind is measured without any wind instrument at all. The ground station simply watches how far the balloon drifts sideways, and the drift is the wind. What happens on the way up is the elegant part. Air pressure falls as the balloon rises, so the gas inside pushes outward against less and less resistance. The balloon swells. By the time it has passed the cruising altitude of airliners it is no longer the size of a beach ball but the size of a small house, its rubber stretched to a skin thinner than plastic wrap. It keeps going. Somewhere above 100,000 feet, in the thin cold air of the stratosphere, the latex reaches a stretch it cannot survive and tears itself apart. The burst is not a failure. It is the design. A parachute opens, the radiosonde drifts back to Earth, and in the United States only about one in five is ever found and returned. The rest lie in fields and forests and the sea, having already sent everything they knew. Consider what that flight actually buys. Satellites are extraordinary, but a satellite reads the atmosphere from the outside, inferring temperature and moisture from radiation it detects at a distance. The balloon does not infer anything. It is inside the weather, touching it, sampling the real air at every altitude on its way through. Nearly every forecast you have ever been given, every hurricane track, every school snow day, was computed by a model that was fed the numbers those two daily flights brought back. There is no cheaper way to be there, and being there is not optional. So the balloon is a machine with a peculiar contract. It must be strong enough to lift a payload through the entire breathable world and weak enough to shatter at the end of it. It works exactly once. It is thrown away at the edge of space by design, and we build it out of the sap of a tree, and it is the reason anyone can tell you what tomorrow will be like.
